This isolates whether pooling several profiles helps. 3. Why it is the best next run: profile setting is a structural choice that affects about two-thirds of the remaining search space, so its answer guides most later decisions. Moving the PCA RNA model from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool gave a large gain (0.485 to 0.591 accuracy; F1 0.464 to 0.573). Multiprofile is therefore the most promising direction. That isolates the effect of aggregation and shows whether a learned, attention-based summary across profiles adds value beyond simple averaging. 3. It builds directly on the strongest result with a single-variable change, so it tests a likely improvement while also answering a design question. The answer shapes many later choices, because aggregation appears in most of the remaining multiprofile and multimodal configurations. Testing multimodal fusion or other RNA encoders before settling this would leave a key, widely shared factor unresolved.

The experiment therefore exploits the best-known configuration while answering an open question cleanly. The other untested axis, the scVI encoder, can follow, ideally within whichever fusion setting performs better here.

This tells us whether the image-modality gain still holds on top of the stronger scVI representation, or whether scVI already captures most of the useful signal. 3. Why now: It exploits the best-supported settings for representation, profile setting, aggregation and fusion while changing only one factor relative to two existing runs. Either outcome is informative and directly guides the remaining budget, and it is the most likely candidate for a new best.

1) Evidence: scVI is the strongest RNA encoder so far (about 0.650 to 0.653 accuracy), well ahead of PCA (0.591) and scGPT (0.530). Multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile for PCA (0.591 vs 0.485). If fusion helps, the remaining runs can try concat fusion or the ViT-L image encoder. If it does not, the remaining budget can go back to RNA-only refinements.

1) Evidence: multiprofile avgpool beat single-profile and transformer aggregation for RNA, and scVI was the strongest RNA encoder (0.650). 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_037 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. 1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_018 (multiprofile, avgpool, concat, pca_n2000 + resnet50) at 0.619 accuracy and 0.610 F1. Multiprofile clearly beat singleprofile (0.527). 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_037 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion) at 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1. Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (about 0.71–0.72 versus 0.59 for pca_n2000 and 0.52 for scgpt). The image encoder and fusion choices change accuracy by only about 0.004–0.012, which is likely within noise. Aggregation is still a major untested design choice, because every run so far used the transformer. Test: config_012 changes only aggregation (avgpool instead of transformer) from the current best, config_007 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, weighted fusion). This isolates the effect of aggregation. Why now: aggregation is the largest remaining uncertainty near the best region. Avgpool could either beat the transformer or confirm it, and either result tells us how to spend the last 3 experiments.

Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor. scVI reached 0.706-0.725, while PCA reached 0.586 and scGPT 0.520. Image encoder, fusion and aggregation changes within scVI multimodal runs moved accuracy only by about 0.004-0.019. The best so far is config_007 (scVI, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) at 0.725. Why now: with 3 runs left after this one, more small fusion or encoder tweaks to the scVI multimodal setup look unlikely to give large gains. 1) Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. It beat PCA by about 0.14 and scGPT by about 0.20 with everything else held fixed. Around the best run, config_007 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725), other single-factor changes made only small differences: concat gave 0.721, ResNet50 gave 0.713, and avgpool gave 0.706. All these differences are around 0.02 or less, so local tweaks to this configuration are unlikely to produce a meaningful gain. The biggest remaining uncertainty is the profile setting: every multimodal run so far used multiprofile, and singleprofile has never been tested. 2) This experiment keeps the best scVI + ViT-L + weighted setup and switches only to singleprofile. It directly tests whether multiprofile aggregation actually helps or whether a simpler single-profile model does as well or better. 3) With two experiments left, testing this unexplored, high-impact factor gives more information and more upside than another small tweak. If singleprofile does better, the final two runs can refine it, for example with ResNet50 or concat. If it does worse, that confirms multiprofile, and the remaining budget can go to the few untested scVI multiprofile combinations such as config_049.

Evidence: scvi_n200 with multiprofile input and transformer aggregation is clearly the strongest region. The best result is config_007 at 0.725 accuracy, with config_018 at 0.721. Swapping the RNA encoder (scgpt, pca_n2000), using a single profile, or dropping the image modality all hurt by large margins. Within this region the remaining choices are close. Concat vs. weighted fusion differed by only about 0.004 with vit_l. ResNet50 (config_044) lowered accuracy slightly but gave the highest F1 so far (0.695). Avgpool was a little worse than transformer aggregation. Test: config_049 is the only untested transformer variant in this region (scvi_n200 + resnet50 + concat). It checks whether concat fusion pairs better with ResNet50 features than weighted fusion, and could beat 0.725 given ResNet50's stronger F1. Why now: with two experiments left, exploiting the top region is a better use of budget than exploring options that have consistently underperformed. Among the untested neighbours, this one changes only the fusion choice from a strong, high-F1 configuration, so it is the most plausible path to a new best.

1) Evidence: the scvi_n200 + multiprofile + multimodal backbone clearly dominates. The best result is config_007 (ViT-L, transformer, weighted) at 0.725. With ViT-L, concat fusion performed about the same as weighted (0.721 vs 0.725), and avgpool fell only slightly below transformer (0.706). The weaker designs are clearly worse: scGPT and PCA encoders, singleprofile, and rna_only. With ResNet50, concat lost more (0.688 vs 0.713). 2) Test: config_026 is the last untested scvi + ViT-L multiprofile variant (avgpool + concat). It checks whether concat fusion pairs better with mean pooling than with transformer aggregation. 3) Why this one: this is the final experiment, so exploitation is the priority. Among the remaining options, config_026 stays closest to the best-performing region and has the highest expected accuracy. The other scvi options use ResNet50 with avgpool, and history suggests ResNet loses more from these changes. A gain over 0.725 is unlikely, but this gives the best remaining chance.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet, so every design choice is uncertain. Prior expectations favor multimodal, multiprofile models: RNA and image signals are likely complementary, and pooling over multiple profiles should reduce noise. 2. What it tests: This sets a strong but moderately priced baseline in the most promising region. It uses multimodal input, multiprofile avgpool aggregation, a compact scvi_n200 RNA encoder, a ResNet50 image encoder and weighted fusion. Later experiments can change one factor at a time against it: transformer aggregation, ViT-L, scGPT, concat fusion, or a single-modality ablation. 3. Why now: It starts in the likely high-accuracy region without paying for the heaviest components (ViT-L, transformer aggregation, scGPT), so it is an efficient anchor for the remaining 9 experiments. 1. Evidence: we have only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile setup with scVI, ResNet50, avgpool and weighted fusion (config_016) reached 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1 at 5.9 GPU hours. That gives a reasonable baseline but says nothing yet about which component limits performance. 2. Test: config_034 keeps everything the same except the image encoder, swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L. Because only one factor changes, any difference can be attributed to the image encoder. Pretrained image backbones are often among the biggest drivers of accuracy in cell-profiling tasks. The result tells us whether later experiments, such as aggregation, fusion and RNA-encoder variants, should build on ViT-L or ResNet50. 3. Value: this is the highest-leverage early test, combining a plausible accuracy gain with a clean ablation of a major design choice. Expected cost is higher than config_016, roughly 1.3 to 2 times or about 8 to 11 GPU hours, because ViT-L produces larger representations. The cost is justified because this choice shapes the rest of the 8-experiment budget.

1) Evidence: Two multiprofile multimodal runs share scVI RNA, avgpool aggregation and weighted fusion. Swapping the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L raised validation accuracy from 0.678 to 0.706, and F1 rose similarly. It was also cheaper (4.82 vs 5.90 GPU hours). That tells us whether later experiments, such as RNA encoder or fusion variants, should use transformer or avgpool aggregation. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_034, roughly 5 to 7 GPU hours, because of the added transformer aggregation layer. That cost is justified because this is a likely route to the top accuracy.

1) Evidence so far: ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50 (0.706 vs 0.678 with avgpool). Transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706) and was also cheaper (3.6 vs 4.8 GPU h). The RNA encoder is still untested, since every run used scVI. 2) This run keeps the best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, weighted fusion) and swaps scVI for the scGPT foundation-model encoder. 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_033 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer aggregation + weighted fusion), with 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Two choices look fairly well supported. ViT-L beat ResNet50 under avgpool, and transformer aggregation beat avgpool, with F1 agreeing both times. The RNA encoder matters a lot, since scGPT dropped accuracy to 0.52, so scVI is the safe choice. Fusion is still completely untested, because every run so far used weighted fusion. 2. Test: config_027 keeps the best configuration and changes only the fusion to concat. This isolates whether the fusion choice adds accuracy on top of the strongest setup. 3. Why now: Changing one variable from the current best is both the highest-value exploitation and the cleanest way to resolve an open design choice. The alternative, switching to a PCA RNA encoder (config_004), can be tested next. Expected cost is moderate and similar to config_033 (about 3.5 to 4 GPU hours). 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_033 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer aggregation + weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Across the completed runs, ViT-L beat ResNet50 (0.706 vs 0.678) and transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706). Weighted and concat fusion are nearly tied (0.725 vs 0.721), so fusion looks like a minor factor. RNA encoder choice has the largest effect seen so far: scGPT dropped accuracy to 0.520. The pca_n2000 encoder is still completely untested, which is the biggest remaining unknown among the main design choices. 2) This experiment swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000 and keeps the best-known setup otherwise. Whatever the result, the remaining 3 runs can then focus on refinements such as ablations or concat fusion. Expected cost is moderate, roughly 3.5-5 GPU hours, similar to config_033. The 2000-dimensional PCA input may add a little cost compared with the 200-dimensional scVI input.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Within multiprofile multimodal models, scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. With the image side fixed, swapping scvi (0.725) for pca_n2000 dropped accuracy to 0.586 and for scgpt to 0.520. ViT-L beat ResNet50 (0.706 vs 0.678 under avgpool). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706). Weighted and concat fusion are effectively tied (0.725 vs 0.721, F1 0.685 vs 0.681). Because the RNA encoder causes such large swings, RNA appears to drive performance, but we have never measured how much the image modality actually adds. 2. What this tests: an RNA-only, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer model. This is the best known setup with the image branch removed. If it matches or beats 0.725, the image branch adds little or even adds noise. That would point the last two experiments toward unimodal variants. If it falls clearly short, multimodal fusion is confirmed, and the remaining budget can go to fine-tuning around config_033, for example a single-profile or ResNet variant. 3. Why now and cost: this ablation addresses the largest remaining design uncertainty while still having a realistic chance of producing the best result. It should also be cheaper than the multimodal runs (about 3.6–5.9 GPU hours each), likely around 2–3 GPU hours, since it drops the ViT-L image branch and the fusion step.

1) Evidence: scVI RNA with the ViT-L image encoder is clearly the strongest combination so far. config_033 (transformer, weighted) leads at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1, and config_027 (transformer, concat) is close behind at 0.721. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool, ViT-L beat ResNet50, and the scGPT and PCA RNA encoders did much worse. The main design choice never tested is the profile setting: every run so far used multiprofile. 2) Test: config_042 keeps the best encoders and weighted fusion but switches to singleprofile, so it directly measures what multiprofile aggregation contributes. 3) Why now: the other neighbours of the best run are unpromising. ResNet50 variants such as config_025 and config_036 swap in the weaker image encoder, and avgpool variants were already worse. This run instead resolves a major untested choice. Singleprofile skips aggregation over multiple profiles, so I expect it to be cheaper than the multiprofile multimodal runs, roughly 2-3 GPU hours versus 3.6-5.9. If it competes, it opens a cheaper high-accuracy region for the final experiments; if it falls short, it confirms multiprofile with transformer aggregation as the direction to exploit.

1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_033 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer aggregation + weighted fusion, 0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1). Some choices are well supported. scVI clearly beats PCA and scGPT. Multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706). Weighted and concat fusion are about tied (0.725 vs 0.721). The image encoder is the one key choice not yet tested within the best setup. The only ResNet50 result used avgpool, where ViT-L led by about 3 points (0.706 vs 0.678). That gap may change with transformer aggregation, because the encoders could interact with how profiles are combined. 2. What this tests: config_025 changes only the image encoder relative to the best configuration (ViT-L to ResNet50, keeping scVI, transformer and weighted fusion). It shows whether ViT-L's advantage holds with transformer aggregation, or whether ResNet50 features gain more from it. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: The other options look weaker. Concat fusion is roughly tied with weighted, avgpool has already lost to transformer, and image-only or RNA-only models are unlikely to beat multimodal. This is the remaining untested single-factor change around the best configuration with a realistic chance of an improvement. 1) Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder; PCA (0.586) and scGPT (0.520) did much worse. Multiprofile with transformer aggregation is consistently best. The current best is config_033 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725). ResNet50 with transformer and weighted fusion came close (0.713) and had the highest F1 so far (0.695). Concat fusion performed about the same as weighted with ViT-L (0.721 vs 0.725). 2) Test: config_036 is the only untested combination in the strongest region that changes just one factor from config_025, swapping weighted fusion for concat. 1) Evidence: No experiments have been run, so there is no data on which modality, encoder, aggregation or fusion matters. Prior knowledge suggests multimodal, multiprofile models should do best, since they combine RNA and image signals and pool information across profiles. 2) Test: config_030 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000 RNA, resnet50 image, avgpool aggregation, weighted fusion) is a strong but relatively cheap anchor. 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only one result exists. The multimodal multiprofile setup with PCA RNA, ResNet50, avgpool and weighted fusion (config_030) reached 0.639 accuracy and 0.620 F1 for 10.6 GPU hours. That gives a reasonable baseline, but every design choice is still untested. 2. What this tests: config_045 changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps everything else fixed. This gives a clean single-factor comparison of the image backbone. Because the image representation often drives a large share of performance in cellular profiling, this is one of the most important open questions. 3. Why now: If ViT-L helps, it sets the backbone for later tests of aggregation, fusion and RNA encoder. If it does not help, we can stay with the cheaper ResNet50 for the rest of the search. Evidence: the two completed runs share pca_n2000, avgpool and weighted fusion and differ only in image encoder. ResNet50 scored 0.639 and ViT-L 0.635 in accuracy, with F1 of 0.620 and 0.618. That gap is too small to separate them, and ViT-L was cheaper (7.0 vs 10.6 GPU hours), so I keep ViT-L as the default image encoder. Question: aggregation is the largest untested design choice in the multiprofile setting. This run keeps everything from config_045 and swaps avgpool for transformer aggregation, so the change is a clean single-factor test of whether learned aggregation across profiles beats simple pooling. Why now: settling aggregation early tells us which branch to use for the remaining runs on RNA encoder (scgpt or scvi) and fusion type (concat or weighted). Expected cost is moderate, somewhat above the 7.0 GPU hours of config_045 because of the transformer aggregator, and likely still below the 10.6 hours of the ResNet50 run.

1) Evidence: avgpool clearly beat transformer aggregation (0.635 vs 0.586 with the same pca_n2000 + ViT-L + weighted setup). This is one comparison, but the gap is large. Image encoder choice matters little: ResNet50 scored 0.639 and ViT-L 0.635, a difference within noise, and ViT-L was cheaper (7.0 vs 10.6 GPU h). The RNA encoder has never been varied; every run so far used pca_n2000. 2) This experiment keeps the best known backbone (multiprofile, avgpool, weighted fusion, ViT-L) and swaps pca_n2000 for scGPT. Fixing the other choices at their best known values means the result directly guides the remaining 6 experiments, for example whether to try scVI next or switch to tuning fusion. scvi_n200 (config_041) would be the cheaper way to test the RNA encoder, but I chose scGPT because I expect it is the more likely of the two to beat PCA. Expected cost: moderate, roughly similar to config_045 (~7–9 GPU h). It is cheaper than the ResNet50 variant, though scGPT embeddings may add some overhead.

1) Evidence so far: among multiprofile multimodal runs, the RNA encoder has the largest observed effect. pca_n2000 reached about 0.635-0.639, while scgpt reached 0.542 under otherwise identical settings. avgpool clearly beat transformer aggregation (0.635 vs 0.586). ResNet50 and ViT-L are close (0.639 vs 0.635), and the ViT-L run cost less (7.0 vs 10.6 GPU h). Because one factor changes, it shows directly whether scvi can match or beat pca_n2000 on the factor that has mattered most. 3) It is the best use of the next slot because an untested RNA encoder carries the largest remaining uncertainty and potential upside, given how strongly this factor has moved accuracy. The concat-versus-weighted fusion question can follow on the winning encoder. Expected cost is relatively low, roughly at or below config_045's 7 GPU h, since scvi's 200-dimensional input is smaller than PCA's 2000 and ViT-L has been cheaper here than ResNet50.

1) Evidence: the RNA encoder is the strongest factor so far. scvi_n200 reached 0.706 accuracy and 0.667 F1, compared with about 0.635 for pca_n2000 and 0.542 for scGPT, all with ViT-L, avgpool and weighted fusion. 1) Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. scvi_n200 reached 0.706 to 0.715 accuracy, while pca_n2000 reached about 0.635 to 0.639 and scgpt reached 0.542. 1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder (0.706 and 0.715, versus 0.635 to 0.639 for pca and 0.542 for scgpt). imagenet_vit_l beats resnet50 with scvi (0.715 vs 0.632). 1) Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor. scVI clearly beats PCA and scGPT (0.706–0.715 vs ≤0.639). ViT-L also clearly beats ResNet50 when paired with scVI (0.715 vs 0.632). 1) Evidence: scVI-200 RNA plus ViT-L images, multiprofile, is clearly the strongest region, at 0.706–0.721. Swapping in ResNet50, PCA or scGPT drops accuracy sharply. 1. Evidence so far: the two runs share scvi_n200, ViT-L and concat fusion and differ only in aggregation. 1) Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. Swapping scvi_n200 for scgpt dropped accuracy from about 0.72 to 0.51. If avgpool roughly matches 0.725, later experiments can use the cheaper aggregator while varying the RNA encoder (scGPT, PCA), the image encoder and the fusion method. If avgpool clearly drops, the remaining budget should focus on transformer-based variants. 3) Why now: aggregation is a major, expensive design axis, and this is a controlled one-variable ablation of the current best. 1) Evidence: there are only two runs so far. Both are multimodal multiprofile models with scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l and weighted fusion. Transformer aggregation (config_010: acc 0.725, F1 0.685) beat avgpool (config_047: acc 0.706, F1 0.667) on both metrics, and it also cost less (3.60 vs 4.82 GPU h). Transformer aggregation is therefore the provisional choice, though one comparison is weak evidence. The RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion type are still completely untested. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the RNA encoder from scvi_n200 to scGPT. That isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation improves on scVI latents, which is plausibly the biggest remaining source of accuracy. 3) It exploits the current best setup while answering a major open design question with a clean one-factor comparison. Its result will guide the following runs, which can test concat fusion and a resnet50 image encoder. Expected cost is similar to or slightly above config_010, roughly 3.5–4.5 GPU hours, because scGPT embeddings may be larger. That is moderate and justified by the potential gain.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_010 (scVI-n200, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 accuracy. Changing only the RNA encoder to scGPT (config_014) dropped accuracy to 0.520, so the RNA encoder looks like the most influential design choice. Switching to avgpool (config_047) cost only about 0.019 accuracy, so aggregation looks less influential. The third RNA option, pca_n2000, is still untested. Test: config_048 keeps the best setup (ViT-L, transformer, weighted) and swaps scVI for pca_n2000. This shows whether scVI is truly the best RNA encoder or whether PCA features can match or beat it. Why now: settling the highest-impact axis first makes the later fusion and image-encoder comparisons (concat, resnet50) more reliable. Expected cost: similar to config_010, roughly 3.5–4.5 GPU hours. It may be slightly higher because the PCA input is wider (2000 dimensions), but it should be well below a hypothetical larger architecture.

1) Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (0.725 vs 0.586 for PCA and 0.520 for scGPT). Transformer aggregation slightly beats avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706), and its F1 agrees. Fusion has never been varied, though: every run so far used weighted fusion, so it is the largest untested design choice next to the best setup. 2) This run keeps the best configuration (scVI, ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer) and changes only the fusion to concat. That isolates the fusion effect, either finding a better model or confirming weighted fusion. 3) It is a direct, low-risk extension of the leading setup and settles an important axis early, which leaves the remaining budget for the image-encoder choice (ResNet50 vs ViT-L) or unimodal checks. 1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (about 0.72 accuracy, versus 0.59 for pca_n2000 and 0.52 for scgpt). 1) Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor. scvi_n200 reached 0.70-0.725, while pca_n2000 reached 0.586 and scgpt 0.520. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706). Weighted vs concat fusion (0.725 vs 0.721) and vit_l vs resnet50 (0.725 vs 0.713) made only small differences. Because the image encoder barely changes results, it is unclear whether the image modality adds anything over scvi RNA features. 2) This experiment keeps the best settings (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer) and drops images. If RNA-only matches or beats 0.725, it could become the best configuration and would point the last experiments toward RNA-centric variants. 1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder, ahead of pca_n2000 (0.586) and scgpt (0.520). Transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706). Weighted vs concat fusion and ViT-L vs ResNet50 differ by only about 0.4-1.2 points, so the best-so-far config_010 (scvi + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725) sits near the top of that neighbourhood. Evidence: the strongest settings are scVI-n200 with multiprofile transformer aggregation. Best so far is config_010 (ViT-L, weighted, 0.725), with concat close behind (config_024, 0.721). Within noise, the image encoder and fusion choices look roughly tied. ResNet50 with weighted fusion (config_020) had slightly lower accuracy (0.713) but the highest F1 (0.695). Expected cost is relatively high, about 5–6.5 GPU hours, similar to config_020 and config_024, since it is multimodal multiprofile with ResNet50. 1) Evidence: The best result is config_010 at 0.725 accuracy (scVI_n200, ViT-L, transformer, weighted fusion). scVI clearly beats scGPT and PCA. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 0.019, while weighted and concat fusion are nearly tied (0.725 vs 0.721). ResNet50 trails ViT-L slightly on accuracy. 1. No experiments have been run, so all I have are priors. Combining RNA and image modalities and aggregating across multiple profiles with a learned transformer usually helps on cellular profiling tasks. Which RNA encoder and which image backbone work best is still unknown. 2. Config_001 tests a strong-prior design: multimodal, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, concat fusion, the compact scVI (n200) RNA embedding and a ResNet50 image encoder. It gives a high-quality anchor result. Later runs can each change one factor against it: ViT-L vs ResNet50, scGPT/PCA vs scVI, avgpool vs transformer, weighted vs concat fusion, and single-modality ablations. 3. It is likely to perform near the top of the space without paying for ViT-L features up front, so it is a good first use of the budget. Expected relative cost is medium-high. Multiprofile transformer aggregation over two modalities costs more than single-profile or avgpool configs, but the small 200-dim scVI embedding and ResNet50 keep it well below the ViT-L multimodal transformer variants.

1) Evidence: only one result exists so far. config_001 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + resnet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1 at 5.16 GPU hours. With a single point, we cannot yet tell which design choices drive performance. 2) Test: config_030 changes only the image encoder, from resnet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, and keeps everything else fixed. The image encoder is likely one of the most influential choices in multimodal cellular profiling. 3) Why now: a single-factor change from the only known reference point makes the result directly interpretable. If it does not, we can safely stay with the cheaper resnet50 and turn to the RNA encoder (scGPT), aggregation or fusion choices. That cost is justified because this variant is a strong candidate for the best-performing configuration.

1. Evidence: Two experiments so far. Both are multimodal, multiprofile, with a transformer aggregator, concat fusion and the scvi_n200 RNA encoder. Swapping the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l raised accuracy from 0.688 to 0.721 and F1 from 0.659 to 0.681. ViT-L is also slightly cheaper (4.65 vs 5.16 GPU hours), so config_030 is the current best and anchor. The RNA encoder, fusion type and aggregation are all still untested, and the RNA encoder is probably the biggest open question. 2. Test: config_005 changes only one factor from config_030, replacing scvi_n200 with the pretrained scgpt RNA encoder. This shows whether a foundation-model RNA representation improves on scVI within the best setup found so far. 3. Why now: this exploits the ViT-L result while resolving a high-impact design choice. A clean one-factor comparison keeps the result interpretable for later fusion and aggregation tests (e.g., config_010, config_034, config_011). Expected cost: similar to or slightly above config_030, roughly 5 GPU hours, since scGPT embeddings may be somewhat larger than scVI's 200 dimensions.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_030 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. ViT-L beat ResNet50 by about 3 points. The RNA encoder had the largest effect: swapping scVI for scGPT dropped accuracy to 0.507. The third RNA option, PCA-2000, is untested, so the biggest open uncertainty is on the factor that matters most. 2) Test: This run keeps the best setup fixed (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, concat) and swaps only the RNA encoder to PCA-2000. That cleanly isolates the encoder effect and could find a stronger RNA representation than scVI. 3) Why now: Ranking the RNA encoders fully is the most valuable step before tuning secondary choices with the remaining 6 runs. Evidence: across the four multiprofile transformer-concat runs, scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (0.721 vs 0.599 for pca_n2000 and 0.507 for scgpt). With scvi, imagenet_vit_l beat resnet50 (0.721 vs 0.688), and F1 agrees. 1. Evidence: The scvi_n200 RNA encoder is clearly best (0.72 vs 0.60 for pca_n2000 and 0.51 for scgpt). imagenet_vit_l beats resnet50 (0.721 vs 0.688). 1. Evidence: The best result so far is config_034 (scVI-n200 + ViT-L, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Test: config_031 keeps the winning encoders and weighted fusion but uses a single profile with no aggregation. This shows whether multiprofile aggregation actually helps. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_034 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. The RNA encoder is the most influential choice: with ViT-L and transformer aggregation held fixed, scVI reached 0.72, PCA 0.60 and scGPT 0.51. Swapping the image encoder changed accuracy less, from 0.69 with ResNet50 to 0.72 with ViT-L. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706), and multiprofile beat singleprofile by a wide margin. The untested question is whether the image branch adds much, or whether the scVI RNA signal carries most of the performance. 2) This experiment runs RNA-only scVI with multiprofile transformer aggregation, the strongest RNA and aggregation settings, without the image branch. If it comes close to or beats 0.725, image fusion may be adding noise. 1. Evidence: The best result is config_034 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Nearby variants already show what matters. Weighted vs concat fusion gives only small gains (+0.004). Transformer beats avgpool (+0.019). ViT-L beats ResNet50 (+0.033 under concat). Multiprofile beats singleprofile by a wide margin. Weak RNA encoders hurt badly (scGPT 0.507, PCA 0.599), even below scVI RNA-only (0.653). So the untested neighbours of config_034 are predictable and probably slightly worse: config_025 (ResNet50) at about 0.69 and config_011 (avgpool) at about 0.70. The open question is how much the ViT-L image branch delivers on its own. It has never been tested alone. Since poor RNA features can drag the multimodal model down, image-only multiprofile with transformer aggregation might be competitive with the best result.
2. What it tests: This measures the standalone contribution of the image modality under the best aggregation setting. It clarifies whether the RNA branch adds real signal or whether image features drive most of the accuracy.
3. Why it is the best use of the budget: It is the most uncertain option with real upside, whereas exploiting further around config_034 is very likely to land below it. The last experiment can then refine based on the answer. Expected cost is moderate, likely below the roughly 3.6–4.8 GPU hours of the multimodal multiprofile runs because there is no RNA branch or fusion.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_034 (scVI-n200 + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. The search has established that multiprofile beats singleprofile, multimodal beats either single modality, scVI is the best RNA encoder by a wide margin, and transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706). Weighted fusion is slightly better than concat, though that gap is small. One dimension is still unresolved inside the winning recipe: the image encoder has only been compared under concat fusion, where ResNet50 scored 0.688 and ViT-L 0.721. 2) This experiment: config_025 keeps everything from the best recipe and swaps in ResNet50. 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet on modality, profile setting, encoders, aggregation or fusion. 2) What this tests: config_031 is a mid-cost anchor for the region most likely to perform well: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 RNA latents, ResNet50 image features, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion. The prior that this region is strong comes from general expectations (combining modalities and aggregating profiles often helps), not from data in this study. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_050 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted fusion, 0.725 acc, 0.685 F1). Among the design choices, scVI clearly beats PCA and scGPT, and transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632 with ResNet50). Multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile. ViT-L beat ResNet50 by about 0.033 under concat fusion. Weighted fusion gave a small gain over concat with ViT-L. 2) Test: config_008 keeps every winning choice (scVI, transformer, multiprofile, weighted fusion) and only swaps the image encoder to ResNet50. This checks whether weighted fusion closes the image-encoder gap. ResNet50 is the one strong-component alternative not yet paired with weighted fusion. 3) Why this is the best final use: every other untested option includes a choice already shown to be clearly inferior (avgpool, PCA, scGPT, singleprofile or unimodal). This makes config_008 the remaining configuration with the best realistic chance of matching or beating 0.725. Expected cost is moderate, about 4-5 GPU hours, similar to the other multiprofile transformer runs (3.6-5.2 GPU hours).

1) No experiments have been completed, so there is no evidence on modality, profile setting, encoders, aggregation or fusion. Priors suggest that multimodal inputs, multiprofile context and learned (transformer) aggregation are the most likely high-accuracy structure. Encoder choice is the most uncertain factor. 2) Config_003 tests that likely-strong structure (multimodal, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) using the compact scVI-200 RNA embedding and ResNet50 images. It gives a strong anchor to compare against later. Next steps can include single-modality or singleprofile ablations, avgpool vs transformer, and upgrades to scGPT or ViT-L. 3) It probes the most promising region without paying for the largest encoders up front. Expected cost is moderate: multiprofile aggregation plus multimodal processing, but with smaller representations. It should be noticeably cheaper than ViT-L or scGPT variants such as config_015.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_003 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + resnet50, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) reached 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1 for 6.22 GPU hours. A single point says nothing yet about which components drive performance. 2) This experiment keeps everything fixed except the image encoder, swapping resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l. It cleanly tests whether a larger pretrained image representation improves accuracy. The image encoder is likely one of the most influential design choices, and the answer will guide the image-side choice for the remaining multimodal and image-only configurations. 3) It changes one factor around the current best, so it both explores and exploits, and it has a good chance of producing a new best. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_003, roughly 1.3-1.6x or about 8-10 GPU hours, because ViT-L is larger. That cost is justified because this encoder is plausibly part of the top-performing configuration.

1. Evidence: Only two experiments are done, and both used scVI RNA, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion. Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L raised validation accuracy from 0.713 to 0.725 and cut cost from 6.22 to 3.60 GPU hours. F1 was slightly lower (0.685 vs 0.695), so the image-encoder advantage is real but modest. The largest open uncertainty is the RNA encoder, since only scVI has been tried. 2. Test: Keep the current best setup (ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer, weighted fusion) and swap scVI for scGPT. This isolates whether a foundation-model RNA encoder improves the RNA side of the fusion. 3. Why now: A one-factor change on the leading configuration both exploits the best result and resolves a major untested design axis. If scGPT helps, later runs can tune aggregation and fusion around it. If not, pca_n2000 or the scVI fusion and aggregation variants are next. Expected cost is moderate: similar to or somewhat above config_018's 3.6 GPU hours, because scGPT embeddings are larger, but likely below config_003's 6.2.

1) Evidence: the RNA encoder is the factor with the largest observed effect so far. With the same vit_l, transformer and weighted backbone, scvi_n200 reached 0.725 accuracy while scgpt reached only 0.520. The image encoder mattered much less: vit_l was slightly better than resnet50 on accuracy (0.725 vs 0.713) and was cheaper (3.6 vs 6.2 GPU h). pca_n2000 is the only RNA encoder not yet tested. 2) Test: config_002 keeps the best configuration (config_018) fixed and swaps scvi_n200 for pca_n2000. This shows whether a simpler PCA representation matches or beats scVI. 3) Why now: settling the most influential design choice early decides which RNA encoder anchors the later aggregation and fusion tests (avgpool vs transformer, concat vs weighted). It also has a real chance of producing a new best. Expected cost is moderate, about 3-4.5 GPU hours, similar to config_018 and well below the resnet50 run. The 2000-dimensional PCA input may add a little cost.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder so far (0.713–0.725 accuracy, versus 0.586 for pca_n2000 and 0.520 for scgpt). The two image encoders are close: imagenet_vit_l has slightly higher accuracy (0.725) and resnet50 slightly higher F1. Vit_l was also cheaper here (3.60 vs 6.22 GPU hours). All four runs used transformer aggregation with weighted fusion, so aggregation and fusion are completely untested. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup so far (scvi_n200, vit_l, weighted fusion) and changes only aggregation from transformer to avgpool. That isolates whether the transformer aggregator is actually needed. 3) Aggregation is a major untested design choice, and a clean single-variable comparison against the current best will guide the remaining 5 experiments. Fusion can be tested next with config_042 or a concat counterpart. Expected cost is low: avgpool should be cheaper than transformer aggregation, so likely under the 3.6 GPU hours of config_018.

1) Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, at 0.713–0.725 versus 0.586 for PCA and 0.520 for scGPT. The best result so far is config_018 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725 accuracy). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool with this setup (0.725 vs 0.706), and its F1 was also higher. ViT-L and ResNet50 were close (0.725 vs 0.713), and ViT-L was cheaper. The fusion method is the one major design choice never tested: every run so far used weighted fusion. 2) This experiment: config_042 keeps the best setup and changes only fusion to concat. It isolates whether concat fusion can beat weighted fusion. 3) Why now: it directly exploits the leading configuration while closing the largest remaining uncertainty, so the result is easy to interpret. It also tells the remaining 3 experiments whether to keep weighted fusion. Expected cost is moderate, similar to config_018 at about 3.5–5 GPU hours, since concat fusion adds little overhead compared with weighted fusion.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder (0.71-0.725 vs 0.52 for scgpt and 0.59 for pca). Within the scvi multiprofile family, the best result is 0.725 for config_018 (ViT-L, transformer, weighted fusion). Swapping in concat (0.721), ResNet50 (0.713) or avgpool (0.706) gave only small drops, so local tuning around config_018 is close to exhausted. The main untested choice is modality: all six runs were multimodal, so we do not know how much the image branch actually adds. 2) This test: an RNA-only model with scvi_n200 and transformer aggregation over multiple profiles. It shows whether the RNA signal alone matches or beats the multimodal best (the image features may add noise) or falls clearly short (the image branch is necessary). That decides how to spend the last two runs: on image and fusion variants, or on RNA-only and profile-setting variants. 3) Why now: it addresses the largest remaining uncertainty and has a realistic chance of reaching about 0.72 or more, since scvi drives performance. With no image encoder it should be cheaper than the multimodal runs, roughly 2-3 GPU hours versus 3.6-6.2.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_018 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted fusion, 0.725 accuracy, 3.6 GPU h). Swapping single components around it changes accuracy only slightly: concat fusion gave 0.721, ResNet50 gave 0.713 and avgpool gave 0.706. scGPT and PCA RNA encoders were clearly worse. The profile setting has never been tested; every multimodal run so far used multiprofile. 2) Test: config_037 keeps the best encoders and fusion but uses single-profile input with no aggregation. This isolates whether multiprofile aggregation is really needed. It is the main remaining unexplored design axis, and the single-profile model could match or beat the current best. 3) Value: The other close neighbours (ResNet50 + concat, avgpool + concat) recombine choices already shown to be slightly inferior, so they are unlikely to set a new best. This run should be cheaper than the multiprofile runs, roughly 1.5–3 GPU h, because there is no aggregation over profiles. Its result will also guide the last two experiments: refine around single-profile if it is competitive, otherwise around the multiprofile config_018.

1. Evidence: The strongest region is clear. scVI beats pca_n2000 by about 0.14 and scGPT by about 0.20. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool by about 0.019. Multiprofile beats singleprofile by about 0.19, and multimodal beats RNA-only by about 0.07. Within this region, the best result is config_018 (ViT-L, weighted, 0.725). The neighbouring configs config_042 (ViT-L, concat, 0.721) and config_003 (ResNet50, weighted, 0.713) score within about 0.012 of it. Those gaps are small enough to fall within run-to-run noise. 2. What it tests: config_033 (scVI + ResNet50 + transformer + concat) is the only untested scVI/transformer/multiprofile multimodal combination. It completes the image-encoder by fusion comparison, showing whether ResNet50 pairs better with concat fusion than with weighted fusion. 3. Why it is the best use of the slot: every other remaining option drops at least one component that clearly helped. Those are either scGPT or PCA instead of scVI, avgpool instead of transformer, singleprofile, or a single modality, so they are unlikely to beat 0.725. This makes config_033 the highest-probability, if modest, chance of a new best. Expected cost is relatively high, around 5-6 GPU hours, similar to config_003 (6.22 h). That is justified because it is the remaining candidate most likely to compete for the top spot.

1) Evidence: the strongest region is clear. It is multimodal, multiprofile, with an scVI-n200 RNA encoder and an ImageNet ViT-L image encoder. The best run is config_018 (transformer, weighted) at 0.725, followed by config_042 (concat) at 0.721 and config_016 (avgpool) at 0.706. Swapping in scGPT or PCA for RNA dropped accuracy sharply (0.52–0.59). Single-profile and RNA-only runs were also clearly worse, and ResNet50 is slightly behind ViT-L. 2) This experiment: config_007 is the only untested scVI + ViT-L multiprofile combination left. It tests avgpool aggregation together with concat fusion. That combination has not been run, and fusion choice could interact with how profiles are pooled. 3) Why it is the best final use: it stays in the proven high-accuracy region, so it is the most plausible way to match or slightly beat 0.725. The alternatives look weaker. Image-only or other-encoder options have weak or negative evidence, and the remaining scVI + ResNet50 avgpool variants pair the weaker image encoder with the weaker aggregation. Expected cost is moderate, around 4.5–5 GPU hours, similar to config_016 and config_042.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so every design choice is uncertain. These choices are modality, single vs. multiple profiles, RNA and image encoder, aggregation and fusion. Prior expectation is that combining both modalities and aggregating multiple profiles should give the strongest signal, but this is unconfirmed here. 2. What it tests: config_001 is a multimodal, multiprofile setup built from the cheaper components: scVI-200 RNA embeddings, a ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation and simple concat fusion. Its accuracy will show whether the multimodal + multiprofile direction is promising before paying for more expensive parts. 3. Why now: It is a mid-cost anchor that later experiments can compare against by changing one factor at a time. Candidate swaps include ViT-L for ResNet50, transformer for avgpool, weighted for concat, scGPT or PCA for scVI, and single-modality ablations. This leaves 9 experiments to exploit what it reveals. Expected relative cost: moderate. It costs more than single-profile or unimodal runs because of multiprofile and multimodal processing, but clearly less than ViT-L or transformer-aggregation variants.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile config_001 (scVI-200 RNA, ResNet50 images, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1 at 7.27 GPU hours. That gives a reasonable baseline in what is probably the strongest region of the space, but every design axis is still untested. 2) Test: config_049 changes exactly one factor, swapping avgpool for transformer aggregation. Any difference can therefore be attributed to how the multiple profiles are combined. A learned, attention-based aggregator could plausibly beat mean pooling, while the RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion choices stay fixed. 3) Why now: aggregation is likely a high-impact choice that affects many of the remaining multiprofile configurations, so settling it early guides much of the remaining 8-experiment budget. Swapping in the ViT-L image encoder instead would likely cost more. Expected cost: moderately higher than config_001 because of the transformer aggregator, roughly 8-10 GPU hours, which is less than the larger-encoder alternatives.

Evidence: with everything else held fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, concat), transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool on both accuracy (0.688 vs 0.632) and F1 (0.659 vs 0.607). It was also cheaper (5.16 vs 7.27 GPU h), so transformer aggregation is the current anchor. The image encoder is still untested and is a high-impact choice, since ViT-L representations are much richer than ResNet50. This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_049) and changes only the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l. That cleanly measures the encoder's effect and exploits the strongest known direction. It is the best use of a limited budget because the encoder choice likely moves accuracy more than fusion type, and the answer shapes most of the remaining search. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_049, roughly 1.3-1.8x, because ViT-L features are larger, though transformer aggregation should keep it under about 8 GPU h. If the gain is small, later experiments can return to cheaper ResNet50 variants such as weighted fusion or scGPT.

1) Evidence: with the scVI RNA encoder and concat fusion fixed, transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632 with ResNet50). Swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L under transformer aggregation raised accuracy to 0.721 (F1 0.681), the current best (config_018). Fusion has never been varied: every run used concat. The RNA encoder alternatives (PCA, scGPT) are also untested. 2) Test: config_007 matches the best configuration except for weighted fusion instead of concat. This one-factor change isolates the effect of fusion on top of the strongest setup, and F1 can confirm whether any gain is real. 3) Why now: it directly exploits the best configuration found so far while resolving an unexplored design choice that affects every future multimodal candidate. Weighted fusion only adds learned modality weights to the same encoders, so I expect it to cost about the same as config_018 (roughly 4.5-5.5 GPU hours). That is cheaper than the avgpool baseline run and no more expensive than switching to a heavier encoder such as scGPT, which can be tested next on whichever fusion wins.

1. Evidence: Every run so far uses the scvi_n200 RNA encoder. Three image/aggregation/fusion choices have clear evidence. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 5.6 points (0.688 vs 0.632). ViT-L beat ResNet50 by about 3.3 points (0.721 vs 0.688). Weighted fusion edged out concat (0.725 vs 0.721, with F1 also slightly higher), though that gap is small. The biggest untested axis is the RNA encoder. 2. Test: config_024 keeps the best-known setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, weighted fusion) and swaps in scGPT. Changing only one factor isolates whether a pretrained single-cell foundation model improves the RNA representation over scvi_n200. 3. Why now: this extends the strongest direction while reducing uncertainty on the main open design choice. If scGPT helps, the remaining budget can refine around it. If it does not, pca_n2000 (config_005) is the natural next comparison. Expected cost: similar to or somewhat above config_007 (3.6 GPU hours), roughly 4-6 GPU hours, because scGPT embeddings may be larger. That still stays within the range of earlier runs.

1) Evidence: transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632 with resnet50). imagenet_vit_l beats resnet50 (0.721 vs 0.688). Weighted fusion is slightly ahead of concat (0.725 vs 0.721), a small difference. Swapping the RNA encoder to scgpt in the best setup collapsed accuracy to 0.520, so the RNA encoder is a high-impact choice. pca_n2000 is the only RNA encoder not yet tested. 2) config_005 keeps the best setup (multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) and changes only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. This shows whether scvi_n200 is truly the best RNA representation or whether a higher-dimensional PCA input does better. 3) It is the factor with the largest remaining uncertainty and a plausible chance of a new best result, while staying in the strongest region of the search space. Expected cost is moderate, roughly 3.5-5 GPU hours, similar to config_007. The 2000-dimensional PCA input may add a little cost over the 200-dimensional scVI input, but no image-side cost is added.

1) Evidence: every run so far has used multiprofile. The best result is config_007 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, acc 0.725, F1 0.685). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 0.06, ViT-L beat ResNet50, and weighted fusion was slightly ahead of concat. scVI is clearly the best RNA encoder, well ahead of PCA (0.586) and scGPT (0.520). 2) Untested choice: whether to aggregate across multiple profiles at all. This run keeps the strongest components (scVI, ViT-L, weighted fusion) and switches to singleprofile, which directly tests that axis. avgpool variants such as config_012 are unlikely to win given the earlier aggregation gap. 3) Why now: single-profile models skip the costly aggregation step, so this should be the cheapest multimodal run yet, likely below the roughly 3.6 to 4.7 GPU hours of earlier ViT-L runs. If it matches or beats config_007, the last runs can focus on cheaper single-profile variants. If it falls short, it confirms multiprofile with transformer as the backbone, and I would use the final runs to test image-only and RNA-only references (configs 029 and 040).

Evidence: the best result so far is config_007 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1). Within this neighbourhood, scVI clearly beats scGPT and PCA, ViT-L beats ResNet50, and weighted fusion edges concat by a small margin. The weakest-tested choice in the top region is aggregation. Transformer beat avgpool only once, with ResNet50 and concat fusion (0.688 vs 0.632), and avgpool was never tried with ViT-L features. This experiment keeps the best configuration and swaps transformer for avgpool. It checks whether that earlier gap holds with the stronger image encoder, since richer ViT-L embeddings could make simple pooling competitive or better. It is the most direct exploit-plus-uncertainty test left, and the other neighbours (ResNet50, PCA, scGPT, single-profile) already have strong negative evidence. Expected cost is moderate to high, roughly 4–7 GPU hours. That is similar to the earlier multiprofile runs, and the one avgpool run (config_001) cost more than the transformer runs. The cost is acceptable because this is one of the few remaining candidates with a real chance of beating 0.725.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_007 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1). Its close neighbours scored slightly lower: concat fusion gave 0.721 and avgpool aggregation gave 0.706. Switching to ResNet50 cost about 0.03 and multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile. So the remaining multimodal variants (config_044, config_026) are likely to land around 0.69 to 0.71 and unlikely to beat the best. The main untested question is how much each modality contributes. Swapping scVI for scGPT or PCA cut accuracy sharply (0.52 and 0.59), and weighted fusion did not protect against this. That shows the RNA branch strongly shapes results, but we still do not know whether a ViT-L image-only model is competitive. 2) This experiment tests image-only ViT-L with multiprofile transformer aggregation, the strongest image-side setup. It shows whether RNA adds signal on top of the images or only adds noise. 3) It is the only remaining option with a plausible chance of exceeding 0.725, and it informs how to use the final experiment. Expected cost is low to moderate (about 2 to 3.5 GPU hours), below the full multimodal runs, because no RNA branch or fusion is trained.

1) Evidence: the best result is config_007 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Each design choice is fairly well supported. scVI beats PCA and scGPT, ViT-L beats ResNet50, transformer beats avgpool, and multiprofile beats singleprofile. The remaining multimodal neighbours of the best config look unlikely to beat it, since each swaps in a component that has already underperformed (e.g., config_044 uses ResNet50, config_026 uses avgpool). The main open question is how much the image branch actually contributes. Image-only reached just 0.26, which suggests the signal is dominated by RNA and that the image features may add little or even noise. 2) Test: config_040 is RNA-only with scVI and transformer aggregation over multiprofile input. It isolates the strongest RNA pathway and shows whether dropping the weak image modality matches or exceeds 0.725. 3) Why this is the best final use: it is the only remaining option with a realistic chance of beating the current best that does not reuse a component already shown to be worse. It is also expected to be among the cheapest multiprofile runs, roughly 1.5–3 GPU hours, well below the 3.6–7 hours of the multimodal runs. If it falls short, config_007 remains the best.

1. Evidence: no experiments have been run yet, so we have no data on any design factor (modality, single vs. multi-profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation, fusion). 2. What this tests: config_036 is a central anchor. It is multimodal and multiprofile, which I expect to be competitive, and uses a mid-sized RNA encoder (scVI with 200 dimensions) and a strong image encoder (ImageNet ViT-L). It also uses the simplest aggregation (average pooling) and the simplest fusion (concatenation). This gives a reasonably strong first result without committing to the more complex transformer aggregation or weighted fusion. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: later experiments can change one factor at a time from this anchor. That includes switching to RNA-only or image-only, to single-profile, to transformer aggregation, to weighted fusion, or to a different encoder. Each of these comparisons then isolates the effect of one design choice, which is more informative under a limited budget than starting from a minimal baseline far from the likely optimum.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: There is only one result so far. config_036 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) reached 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. We do not yet know how much of this comes from the image branch versus the RNA branch. 2) What this tests: config_005 keeps everything the same except that it removes the image modality (RNA-only, scVI, multiprofile, avgpool). This one-factor change shows directly whether adding images improves on RNA alone. 3) Why now: Whether to use multimodal input is the decision with the widest consequences in this search space. Answering it first tells us whether to spend the remaining budget on fusion, image-encoder and aggregation variants, or on RNA-encoder choices. That makes it a better use of one experiment than fine-tuning secondary settings such as aggregation or fusion type.

Evidence: with the scvi_n200 RNA encoder and avgpool aggregation fixed, multimodal concat with imagenet_vit_l scored 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. RNA-only scored 0.650 accuracy and 0.628 F1, about 6.5 points lower. Uncertainty: we cannot yet tell whether this gain comes from combining the two modalities or simply from the image features alone. Test: image-only imagenet_vit_l with avgpool uses the same image encoder, profile setting and aggregation, so it completes the RNA-only, image-only and multimodal comparison. If image-only is close to 0.715, RNA adds little, and future runs should focus on image encoders and aggregation rather than RNA encoders or fusion. If it is clearly lower, the two modalities are complementary, and tuning fusion, aggregation and RNA encoder within multimodal configurations is justified. Why now: this question decides which design dimensions deserve the remaining budget, so it is a better use of one experiment than a single-dimension tweak of the current best.

1) Evidence: the multimodal model (config_036, scVI + ViT-L, avgpool, concat) scored best at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. RNA-only reached 0.650 and image-only only 0.332, so the RNA signal carries most of the performance and the image adds a meaningful amount on top. Every run so far used avgpool, so we do not know whether aggregation matters. That is a major untested design axis for multiprofile inputs. 2) Test: config_038 changes only avgpool to transformer and keeps the rest of the best configuration fixed. This isolates whether learned, attention-based aggregation across profiles beats simple mean pooling. 3) Why now: it is a one-factor exploitation of the current best direction, so the result is directly interpretable as an aggregation effect. If the transformer helps, it becomes the new base for later tests of the RNA encoder (scGPT, PCA) and the fusion method (weighted). If it does not, we can confidently use the cheaper avgpool for the rest of the budget.

1. Evidence: multimodal models (about 0.715 to 0.721 accuracy) clearly beat RNA-only (0.650) and image-only (0.332). RNA is therefore the dominant signal and images add a useful complement. Aggregation looks like a minor factor: transformer beat avgpool by about 0.006 in accuracy, but avgpool had slightly higher F1, so the result is inconclusive. The RNA encoder has never been varied (only scvi_n200 tested), and RNA carries most of the predictive signal, so this is the largest untested source of uncertainty. 2. This experiment keeps the best multimodal setup (multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) and swaps scvi_n200 for scGPT. Any change can then be attributed to the RNA encoder alone. 3. Under a limited budget, this tests the design choice most likely to move performance substantially and stays within the promising multimodal region. Fusion type and image encoder are worth testing later, but they likely have smaller effects given that the image modality is weak.

1. Evidence: multimodal scVI plus ViT-L is the clear best direction, at about 0.715–0.721 accuracy. It beats RNA-only (0.650) by a wide margin, while image-only is weak (0.332). Avgpool and transformer aggregation are nearly tied: transformer is slightly higher on accuracy, avgpool slightly higher on F1, so aggregation looks minor. scGPT clearly underperforms scVI. Fusion strategy has never been tested; every multimodal run so far used concat. 2. This experiment keeps the best-performing setup (scVI, ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer) and swaps concat for weighted fusion. That isolates the effect of fusion directly. Weighted fusion is a plausible improvement here because the image modality is much weaker than RNA, and learned modality weighting could down-weight noisy image features. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: it builds on the strongest region of the search space and resolves an entirely unexplored design axis with a single controlled comparison. The result will tell us whether fusion should be fixed or explored further before spending runs on secondary axes such as the image encoder or PCA features.

1) Evidence: RNA is the dominant modality. RNA-only scvi reached 0.650, while image-only ViT-L reached only 0.332. The RNA encoder choice has the largest observed effect: swapping scvi for scGPT dropped accuracy from about 0.72 to 0.51. Aggregation and fusion changes within scvi+ViT-L produced only small gains (0.715 to 0.725), and F1 moved inconsistently, so those are fine-tuning details rather than major levers. pca_n2000 is the one RNA encoder never tested. 2) This experiment swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000 in the current best setup (ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion). Comparing it directly with config_039 shows whether scvi is truly the best RNA representation or whether a simpler, higher-dimensional PCA input works as well or better. 3) Because the RNA encoder has the largest demonstrated impact and pca_n2000 is a complete unknown, this test reduces the most important remaining uncertainty. It also has a realistic chance of beating the current best. Testing resnet50 or singleprofile can come next, since the image branch contributes less.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: Several axes are now fairly settled. scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder, at about 0.72 accuracy versus 0.59 for pca_n2000 and 0.51 for scgpt. Multimodal models beat unimodal ones, at 0.72 versus 0.65 for RNA-only and 0.33 for image-only. Aggregation and fusion choices shift results by only about 0.5–1 point, which is within plausible noise. The image encoder is a major axis that has never been varied: every run so far used imagenet_vit_l, which was weak on its own at 0.33. 2. What this tests: config_033 keeps the current best setup (scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) and swaps only the image encoder to resnet50. This isolates whether the choice of image backbone changes the multimodal gain. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: it resolves the largest remaining untested design choice with a clean one-factor comparison against the best run. It also has a real chance of improving on 0.725, so it serves both exploration and exploitation under the limited budget.

1. Evidence so far: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (about 0.72 vs 0.59 for PCA and 0.51 for scGPT). Multimodal beats RNA-only (0.725 vs 0.650). The remaining choices produce only small differences of about 0.01 or less, which are not reliable from single runs: transformer vs avgpool, weighted vs concat, and ViT-L vs ResNet50. The F1 rankings for these choices are also mixed. The biggest untested design choice is the profile setting. Every experiment so far used multiprofile. 2. This experiment keeps the best pipeline (scVI + ViT-L + weighted fusion) and switches to singleprofile. Single-profile runs have no aggregation step, so the only other difference from config_039 (0.725) is that the transformer aggregator is dropped. The comparison therefore shows how much multiprofile aggregation contributes, or whether a simpler single-profile model is competitive. 3. Under a limited budget, resolving an entirely unexplored dimension is worth more than another small tweak among near-equivalent multiprofile settings. It also uses the strongest components, so the run should still perform well.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The broad choices look settled. scVI beats scGPT and PCA, multiprofile beats singleprofile, and multimodal beats RNA-only and image-only. Within the top region (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile), the remaining choices show only small, single-run gaps. avgpool+concat scored 0.715, transformer+concat 0.721 and transformer+weighted 0.725, with F1 roughly flat at 0.681-0.687. It is unclear whether transformer aggregation and weighted fusion each help, or whether they only help together. 2. Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder, ahead of pca_n2000 and scgpt by more than 0.13 accuracy. Multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile (0.725 vs 0.537 accuracy). That makes it more useful than revisiting encoders that already look weak.

The RNA encoder, a major design axis, is still untested: every run so far used scvi_n200. 2. What this tests: config_018 (rna_only, multiprofile, scgpt, avgpool) differs from the strong config_001 baseline only in the RNA encoder. It therefore directly measures whether scGPT embeddings beat scVI. 3. Why it is the best next step: RNA appears to be the dominant signal, so encoder choice is likely to have more effect than further aggregation tweaks. Answering it now also tells us which RNA encoder to carry into later fusion and image experiments, which makes those comparisons more efficient under the limited budget.

1) Evidence: Multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile (0.650 vs 0.520 for scvi RNA-only). The RNA encoder choice has the largest observed effect: scvi_n200 scored 0.650 and scgpt scored 0.530. Aggregation barely matters (avgpool 0.650 vs transformer 0.653). Adding resnet50 images with concat fusion did not help (0.632). The third RNA encoder, pca_n2000, has never been tested. 2) Test: config_024 is identical to config_001 (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) except it uses pca_n2000 instead of scvi_n200. This isolates the effect of the RNA representation. It shows whether a simple high-dimensional PCA input can match or beat scvi. 3) Why now: RNA is currently the strongest signal, and the encoder is the factor with the biggest observed impact. Settling which encoder is best will guide all later multimodal and fusion experiments. It may also find a better baseline.

1. Evidence so far: scVI is clearly the best RNA encoder (0.650 vs 0.591 for PCA and 0.530 for scGPT). Multiprofile beats singleprofile by a wide margin (0.650 vs 0.520). Aggregation matters little (transformer 0.653 vs avgpool 0.650). The one multimodal run (scVI + ResNet50, avgpool, concat; config_031) scored slightly below RNA-only (0.632 vs 0.650 accuracy, with F1 consistent). The open question is whether imaging adds anything. The answer may depend on the image encoder, which is entirely untested beyond ResNet50. 2. This experiment changes only the image encoder relative to config_031, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. Everything else stays fixed: scVI, multiprofile, avgpool, concat. It therefore isolates whether stronger image features make fusion helpful, or whether the multimodal shortfall persists regardless of image representation. 3. Why this is the best next run: the image encoder is the largest remaining unexplored axis, and it determines whether the many multimodal configurations are worth pursuing. Testing weighted fusion first could at best recover RNA-only performance if the image features themselves are weak. A single-factor encoder swap anchored to the best RNA settings is the most informative and lowest-confound use of the budget.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: the best result so far is config_040 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat; 0.715 accuracy). Its counterpart with ResNet50 reached only 0.632, below the RNA-only scVI avgpool model (0.650). So the image encoder clearly matters, but we have no image-only result at all. We cannot tell whether the 0.715 comes from true complementarity between RNA and image, or mostly from ViT-L image features on their own. 2. What this tests: config_021 is the image-only ViT-L model, multiprofile, avgpool. It differs from config_040 only by removing the RNA branch, so it isolates the contribution of fusion. If it matches or beats 0.715, fusion adds little and the search should focus on image-side choices. If it falls well below, combining modalities is justified. 3. Why now: this baseline resolves a central question about the model setting with a single run. It also guides later choices, such as fusion type and aggregation within multimodal models, more efficiently than small extensions of config_040 would.

1. The best result so far is config_040 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat fusion) at 0.715 accuracy. It clearly beats RNA-only scVI (about 0.65) and the ResNet50 multimodal variant (0.63). Aggregation has already been probed: transformer and avgpool were nearly tied in RNA-only (0.653 vs 0.650). Fusion strategy has never been varied, because every multimodal run used concat. 2. config_015 is identical to config_040 except that it uses weighted fusion instead of concat. This isolates the effect of the fusion method within the strongest setting. 3. The choice exploits the most promising direction while resolving the largest remaining unknown with a single-factor change. That makes it more informative than retesting aggregation, where evidence already suggests a small effect, or than lower-performing encoders.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_040 (scVI + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. It beats RNA-only (0.650) and weighted fusion (0.706). scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder and ViT-L beats ResNet50. Aggregation has only been compared in the RNA-only setting, where transformer and avgpool were nearly tied (0.653 vs 0.650). So it is still unknown whether a transformer helps once image features are added. 2) Test: config_029 keeps every setting of config_040 and changes only avgpool to transformer. This isolates the effect of aggregation in the leading multimodal configuration. A learned aggregator might combine cross-profile image and RNA signals better than in the RNA-only case. 3) Why now: it builds directly on the strongest result with a single-variable change, so the outcome is easy to interpret. If it improves, transformer aggregation becomes the new lead. If it does not, avgpool is confirmed as sufficient, and the remaining budget can go to the profile setting or alternative encoders.

1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet about modality, profile setting, aggregation, fusion or encoder choice. 2) This run sets a simple reference point: RNA-only, single profile, PCA encoder, no aggregation and no fusion. It shows how much accuracy and F1 a basic setup achieves before any added complexity. 3) It is the best first use of the budget because many configurations differ from it in exactly one design choice. These include multiprofile with avgpool (config_030), the scVI or scGPT encoders (config_045, config_046) and adding a ResNet50 image encoder with concat fusion (config_012). Later experiments can therefore attribute gains to single changes rather than to many confounded ones. It also avoids assuming that multimodal or multiprofile models are better.

1. Evidence: there is only one result so far, an RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline at 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. We know nothing yet about the image modality, multiprofile aggregation or other RNA encoders. 2. Test: config_049 keeps the RNA encoder and profile setting the same and adds image features (ImageNet ViT-L) through simple concat fusion. This directly measures whether imaging adds information beyond RNA. 3. Why now: whether to use the second modality is probably the most important design choice in this space, and the answer shapes how the remaining budget should be spent. Using single-profile data and the simplest fusion keeps the comparison clean. Profile setting, aggregation and encoder choice can then be tested in later one-factor experiments.

Evidence: in the single-profile setting with PCA RNA features, adding ImageNet ViT-L image features via concat fusion raised validation accuracy from 0.485 to 0.535, and F1 rose in parallel. That gain has two possible explanations. Image features may complement RNA, or images alone may be the stronger signal, with RNA adding little or even diluting it. This experiment tests the image-only single-profile ViT-L model, which completes the modality comparison under identical profile and encoder settings. It will show whether the multimodal gain reflects true fusion benefit or mostly image signal. That answer shapes the rest of the search: either keep investing in fusion and RNA encoder choices, or prioritize image-centric and multiprofile image settings. Under a limited budget, one cheap baseline that removes the main ambiguity in the existing result is worth more than jumping to more complex multiprofile configurations, which would change several factors at once.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is multimodal single-profile PCA plus ViT-L with concat fusion (acc 0.535, F1 0.519). It beats RNA-only (0.485), and image-only is weak (0.227). This suggests RNA carries most of the signal and imaging adds some, but each setting has only one run. Profile setting has not been tested at all, and it is a major design axis. 2) Test: config_027 keeps the best configuration's RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion. It switches only to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool), which multiprofile requires. This gives a near-clean test of whether multiprofile inputs help over single-profile. 3) Why now: it builds directly on the strongest result while answering a large open question. If it helps, transformer aggregation (config_022) is the natural follow-up. If it does not, the budget can move to RNA encoder or fusion comparisons within the single-profile setting.

1. Evidence: Moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised validation accuracy from 0.535 (config_049) to 0.629 (config_027), with F1 rising similarly. Multimodal concat also beat RNA-only (0.485), and image-only was weak (0.227). The strongest signal so far is that multiprofile aggregation matters, but only one aggregation method (avgpool) has been tried. 2. Test: config_022 keeps everything from the current best fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, ViT-L, concat) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. This isolates whether a learned, attention-based aggregation over profiles beats simple averaging. 3. Why now: This extends the most promising direction while varying a single factor, so any change can be attributed to aggregation alone. The answer also guides the remaining search: if the transformer helps, later multiprofile experiments should use it; if it does not, avgpool is a cheaper default. Fusion type and the choice of RNA encoder are good follow-up tests.

1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the dominant modality, with RNA-only at 0.485 versus image-only at 0.227. Adding images helps modestly (0.535 vs 0.485 single-profile). Multiprofile gives the largest gain, with avgpool (0.629) slightly ahead of transformer (0.599). However, every experiment so far has used pca_n2000, so the effect of the RNA encoder is completely unknown, even though RNA carries most of the signal. 2) What this tests: config_007 changes only the RNA encoder (pca_n2000 to scvi_n200) in the current best configuration (multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool, concat). This directly tests whether a learned latent RNA representation improves on PCA. 3) Why it is the best use of budget: this is a one-variable comparison against the best result, on the design axis most likely to matter that has not been explored at all. Either outcome is informative. A gain points to exploiting learned RNA encoders, including scGPT next. No gain supports keeping PCA and turning to fusion type or the RNA-only multiprofile ablation.

1. Evidence: the RNA encoder looks like the strongest lever so far. In the multiprofile, avgpool, concat, ViT-L setting, switching from PCA (config_027, 0.629) to scVI (config_007, 0.715 accuracy, 0.687 F1) gave the largest single-factor gain observed, and F1 moved the same way. scGPT, the third RNA encoder, has not been tested in any configuration, so this is the biggest open uncertainty in the design space. Multiprofile and avgpool are tentatively favoured over singleprofile and transformer, but each rests on only one comparison. 2. Test: config_009 matches the current best setup exactly and changes only the RNA encoder to scGPT. This gives a clean three-way comparison of PCA, scVI and scGPT with everything else held fixed. 3.
